one_liner: Header-only C++ PEG parser-combinator library; its JSON grammar validates 1.7-5.5x faster than nlohmann::json::accept in lexy's benchmark.
what_it_does: PEGTL lets you write a Parsing Expression Grammar directly as C++ types (struct integer : seq< opt< sign >, plus< digit > > {}) and run it with tao::pegtl::parse< Grammar, Action >( input, states... ). There is no generator step or separate lexer: rules, user actions attached by template specialization, control classes, parse-tree building and inputs (memory views, files, mmap, streams) are all library templates. It is a general parsing toolkit, not a JSON library; the measured JSON grammar ships as an example grammar.
how_it_is_fast: Each grammar rule is a type with a static match() function, so a grammar compiles into a hand-written-style recursive-descent parser that the optimizer inlines; the docs say it relies on the compiler for performance and should always be built with inlining enabled. Rules declare a rewind mode so sub-rules can drop their backtracking guards when the caller does not need rewinding, and plain inputs skip line/column bookkeeping. There is deliberately no packrat memoization; the authors argue simple recursive descent usually beats it in practice.
when_to_use: Writing a parser for a custom text format, DSL, config or protocol in C++ without a code-generation step (Bison/ANTLR) and without Boost.
Syntax validation or event-style parsing where you attach actions only to the rules you care about and never build a DOM.
Projects that want a long-lived, BSL-1.0 dependency with released versions, sanitizer and CodeQL CI, and coverage of Linux, macOS, Windows and Android.
Reusing one grammar with different action sets (validate, extract, build a parse tree) through template specialization.
when_not_to_use: JSON specifically: on the same lexy benchmark page it is slower than rapidjson SAX, lexy and glaze on all three files (glaze 3.1-4.4x faster, derived from page data); use a dedicated JSON library.

Grammars that backtrack heavily: there is no memoization (packrat request #35 closed wontfix), so worst-case cost depends entirely on how the grammar is written; the docs tell you to factor out common prefixes.

Untrusted deeply nested input with the default setup: rules recurse on the C++ stack and depth is unbounded unless you opt into the depth limiter (limit_depth in 3.x, check_depth with input_with_depth on main).
Debug or -O0 builds where parser speed matters, and MSVC builds that dislike large object files (the install guide warns /bigobj is often needed).

Codebases that cannot absorb API churn: 4.0.0 (2026-06-07) replaced memory_input/string_input, made parse_error a template and dissolved contrib/, and main is already an unreleased 5.0 requiring C++20.

integration.dependencies: none (ICU optional for Unicode property rules; RTTI used for demangling on compilers other than GCC, Clang and MSVC)
integration.min_toolchain: main (5.0, unreleased): C++20, GCC 11, Clang 13, Visual Studio 2022; 4.x and 3.x branches: C++17; 2.x: C++11
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows, Android; architecture-independent (no SIMD or intrinsics)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; grammars are stateless types and per-run state lives in the input and the state objects you pass to parse()

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the numbers: lexy's benchmarks/json/pegtl.cpp includes tao/pegtl/contrib/json.hpp, constructs pegtl::memory_input and catches the non-template pegtl::parse_error, but PEGTL main dropped memory_input in the input refactor (commit 71e1807, 2023-12-13) and had a templated parse_error by 7ab5fa0 (2025-08-04, the last main commit before the page's 2025-10-13 regeneration); the CMake fetches PEGTL main.zip, so the PEGTL column must come from a cached pre-December-2023 download, the measured version is unknown, and the harness no longer builds as published.

Unequal work against the baseline: nlohmann::json::accept still converts every floating-point token to a double (and, in older versions, every integer), while PEGTL's json::text only checks number syntax, which plausibly explains much of the 5.5x gap on float-heavy canada.json; nlohmann's current develop lexer has since added accept-only shortcuts (discard_number_values, contiguous bulk number scanning), so the ratios are stale.

Parse errors are exceptions by default (global failures from must<>, if_must<>, raise<> and the try_catch rules); -fno-exceptions is supported but those rules are unavailable and file I/O errors call std::perror and std::terminate, so validate-only code typically catches parse_error_base (4.x and later) or parse_error (3.x).

Text inputs track line and column with selectable eol strategies (rule, scan or lazy tracking); plain view/file inputs do not, so choose the input type deliberately when error positions or speed matter.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose PEGTL over lexy when you value a 2007-era, widely used library with semver releases and a large rule, action and parse-tree toolkit over raw speed; lexy validated the same JSON files 1.6-2.2x faster on the same page. Against re2c, PEGTL is a full PEG parser rather than a lexer generator; winnow and chumsky are the Rust counterparts.
verified_claims_summary: In lexy's nanobench JSON validation benchmark on a 2020 M1 Mac Mini (compiler, flags and build type unstated, 11 samples per series), PEGTL's JSON grammar over an in-memory buffer took 3.65/2.37/1.41 ms on canada/citm_catalog/twitter.json versus 20.20/6.60/2.42 ms for nlohmann::json::accept (5.5x/2.8x/1.7x, derived from page data). The PEGTL version measured is unknown (pre-December-2023 main), and PEGTL itself publishes no benchmarks; the maintainers declined to provide performance data in issue #261.
status_note: Actively maintained (4.0.0 released 2026-06-07, 5.0 in progress on main, 2.2k stars, one open issue) under BSL-1.0 and safe to depend on, but pin a release tag since main breaks APIs and requires C++20.
